claim: Homologous recombination helps ensure the timely completion of genome duplication by restarting collapsed replication forks.
source: Homologous recombination helps ensure the timely completion of genome duplication by restarting collapsed replication forks.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Replication restarted by homologous recombination is prone to template switching (TS) that can generate deleterious genome rearrangements associated with diseases such as cancer.
source: However, this beneficial function is not without risk as replication restarted by homologous recombination is prone to template switching (TS) that can generate deleterious genome rearrangements associated with diseases such as cancer.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Nguyen et al., 2015) and represents established knowledge.

claim: TS is detected up to 75 kb downstream of a collapsed replication fork.
source: Here, we show that TS is detected up to 75 kb downstream of a collapsed replication fork and can be triggered by head-on collision between the restarted fork and RNA Polymerase III transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TS can be triggered by head-on collision between the restarted fork and RNA Polymerase III transcription.
source: Here, we show that TS is detected up to 75 kb downstream of a collapsed replication fork and can be triggered by head-on collision between the restarted fork and RNA Polymerase III transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Pif1 DNA helicase, Pfh1, promotes efficient restart.
source: The Pif1 DNA helicase, Pfh1, promotes efficient restart and also suppresses TS.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Pfh1 suppresses TS.
source: The Pif1 DNA helicase, Pfh1, promotes efficient restart and also suppresses TS.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Three conserved helicases (Fbh1, Rqh1 and Srs2) strongly suppress TS.
source: A further three conserved helicases (Fbh1, Rqh1 and Srs2) strongly suppress TS, but there is no change in TS frequency in cells lacking Fml1 or Mus81.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no change in TS frequency in cells lacking Fml1.
source: A further three conserved helicases (Fbh1, Rqh1 and Srs2) strongly suppress TS, but there is no change in TS frequency in cells lacking Fml1 or Mus81.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no change in TS frequency in cells lacking Mus81.
source: A further three conserved helicases (Fbh1, Rqh1 and Srs2) strongly suppress TS, but there is no change in TS frequency in cells lacking Fml1 or Mus81.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Problems that arise during DNA replication are thought to be the root cause of much of the genome instability associated with cancer and other disease states.
source: Problems that arise during DNA replication are thought to be the root cause of much of the genome instability, including duplications, deletions and translocations of chromosomal segments, that is associated with cancer and other disease states (Aguilera and García-Muse, 2013; Arlt et al., 2012; Macheret and Halazonetis, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Accidental collision of the replication fork with proteins that are tightly bound to the DNA is one common problem that arises during DNA replication.
source: One common problem that arises is accidental collision of the replication fork with proteins that are tightly bound to the DNA (Lambert and Carr, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Collisions between replication forks and tightly bound proteins can precipitate replication fork collapse.
source: Such collisions can precipitate a process known as replication fork collapse in which the protein components of the fork (collectively known as the replisome) are thought to partially or completely dissociate from the DNA (Cortez, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: During replication fork collapse, the protein components of the fork are thought to partially or completely dissociate from the DNA.
source: Such collisions can precipitate a process known as replication fork collapse in which the protein components of the fork (collectively known as the replisome) are thought to partially or completely dissociate from the DNA (Cortez, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Replication fork collapse may be associated with DNA breakage, detaching one arm of the replication fork and exposing a single duplex DNA end.
source: In some cases this process may also be associated with DNA breakage, detaching one arm of the replication fork and exposing a single duplex DNA end.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about replication fork collapse.

claim: Replication fork collapse causes a localized cessation of DNA synthesis that can be remedied through the intervention of homologous recombination (HR) proteins, which restart replication.
source: Replication fork collapse, either with or without DNA breakage, causes a localized cessation of DNA synthesis that can be remedied through the intervention of homologous recombination (HR) proteins, which restart replication.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In eukaryotes, recombination-dependent replication (RDR) has been studied mostly in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using experimental systems in which RDR is initiated from a site-specific DNA double-strand break (DSB).
source: In eukaryotes, recombination-dependent replication (RDR) has been studied mostly in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using experimental systems in which RDR is initiated from a site-specific DNA double-strand break (DSB) (Anand et al., 2013; Kramara et al., 2018; Sakofsky and Malkova, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: HR uses intact homologous DNA sequences as templates to repair DSBs.
source: HR uses intact homologous DNA sequences as templates to repair DSBs and, if such sequences are available for only one side of the break, repair occurs via a RDR process termed break induced replication (BIR).
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about homologous recombination.

claim: If homologous DNA sequences are available for only one side of the break, repair occurs via a RDR process termed break induced replication (BIR).
source: HR uses intact homologous DNA sequences as templates to repair DSBs and, if such sequences are available for only one side of the break, repair occurs via a RDR process termed break induced replication (BIR).
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about BIR.

claim: In most cases, BIR has been studied outside of the context of S-phase, with a DSB, rather than a collapsed or broken replication fork, acting as its inducer.
source: In most cases, BIR has been studied outside of the context of S-phase, with a DSB, rather than a collapsed or broken replication fork, acting as its inducer.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about BIR studies.

claim: Studies using a site-specific single-strand DNA break to induce replication fork breakage have shown that essentially the same BIR process can repair broken forks during S-phase.
source: However, studies, using a site-specific single-strand DNA break to induce replication fork breakage, have shown that essentially the same BIR process can repair broken forks during S-phase (Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: BIR involves the 5' to 3' nucleolytic resection of a duplex DNA end to provide a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) tail for the Rad51 recombination protein to load on to.
source: Similar to other HR-mediated repair processes, BIR involves the 5' to 3' nucleolytic resection of a duplex DNA end to provide a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) tail for the Rad51 recombination protein to load on to (Anand et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about BIR.

claim: In yeast, Rad51 loading depends on Rad52, which acts as a mediator between ssDNA coated with the ssDNA-binding protein RPA and Rad51.
source: In yeast, this loading reaction depends on Rad52, which acts as a mediator between ssDNA coated with the ssDNA-binding protein RPA and Rad51 (Krogh and Symington, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Once loaded, Rad51 performs a DNA homology search, followed by strand invasion of the intact DNA sequence that it finds, forming a displacement (D) loop.
source: Once loaded, Rad51 performs a DNA homology search, followed by strand invasion of the intact DNA sequence that it finds, forming a displacement (D) loop.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about Rad51 function.

claim: The D-loop acts as a platform for replication protein reassembly, which seemingly involves most of the main replisome components.
source: The D-loop acts as a platform for replication protein reassembly, which seemingly involves most of the main replisome components (Lydeard et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: BIR exhibits a requirement for the non-essential DNA Polymerase δ subunit Pol32.
source: However, BIR exhibits a number of features that distinguishes it from canonical replication initiated from a replication origin, including: a requirement for the non-essential DNA Polymerase ∂ subunit Pol32 (Lydeard et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lydeard et al., 2007.

claim: BIR exhibits a dependence on the Pif1 DNA helicase to promote DNA synthesis.
source: a dependence on the Pif1 DNA helicase to promote DNA synthesis (Saini et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Saini et al., 2013 and Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: BIR progresses via a migrating D-loop or bubble resulting in conservative rather than semi-conservative replication.
source: progression via a migrating D-loop or bubble resulting in conservative rather than semi-conservative replication (Saini et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saini et al., 2013.

claim: BIR is associated with a massively increased rate of mutagenesis.
source: a massively increased rate of mutagenesis (Deem et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Deem et al., 2011.

claim: BIR is associated with clustered mutations.
source: an association with clustered mutations (Sakofsky et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sakofsky et al., 2014.

claim: BIR is associated with an increased frequency of template switching (TS).
source: and an increased frequency of template switching (TS) (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2007.

claim: A BIR-like process has been documented in human cells.
source: Given that a BIR-like process has been documented in human cells (Costantino et al., 2014; Roumelioti et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Costantino et al., 2014 and Roumelioti et al., 2016.

claim: BIR's error-prone nature and propensity for TS likely causes many of the mutations and genome rearrangements that are associated with cancer and other diseases.
source: it is highly likely that its error-prone nature and propensity for TS causes many of the mutations and genome rearrangements that are associated with cancer and other diseases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the documented properties of BIR and its occurrence in human cells.

claim: A related process to BIR has been documented in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, which is induced by the RTS1 protein-DNA polar replication fork barrier (RFB).
source: We, and others, have documented a related process to BIR in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, which is induced by the RTS1 protein-DNA polar replication fork barrier (RFB), as opposed to a DNA break (Lambert et al., 2010; Miyabe et al., 2015; Mizuno et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations including work from the authors' lab.

claim: Replication forks collapse, and recruit HR proteins, within approximately 10 min of collision with RTS1.
source: Replication forks collapse, and recruit HR proteins, within approximately 10 min of collision with RTS1 (Mohebi et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mohebi et al., 2015 and Nguyen et al., 2015.

claim: Rad51 and Rad52 promote replication restart at RTS1.
source: Similar to BIR, Rad51 and Rad52 promote replication restart at RTS1 and, in doing so, can inadvertently cause genomic rearrangements through the recombination of repetitive DNA elements (Ahn et al., 2005; Lambert et al., 2005; Lambert et al., 2010; Mizuno et al., 2009; Morrow et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rad51 and Rad52 can inadvertently cause genomic rearrangements through the recombination of repetitive DNA elements at RTS1.
source: Similar to BIR, Rad51 and Rad52 promote replication restart at RTS1 and, in doing so, can inadvertently cause genomic rearrangements through the recombination of repetitive DNA elements (Ahn et al., 2005; Lambert et al., 2005; Lambert et al., 2010; Mizuno et al., 2009; Morrow et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RDR induced by RTS1 is highly mutagenic and prone to TS.
source: Also like BIR, RDR induced by RTS1 is highly mutagenic and prone to TS (Iraqui et al., 2012; Mizuno et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Iraqui et al., 2012, Mizuno et al., 2013, and Nguyen et al., 2015.

claim: RTS1 is almost always encountered first by a replication fork moving in the telomere to centromere direction.
source: RTS1 is inserted close to a cluster of early firing replication origins (ori-1323, ori-1338 and ori-1342), which means that it is almost always encountered first by a replication fork moving in the telomere to centromere direction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RTS1 is a polar RFB that only blocks forks at this site in one orientation (active orientation).
source: Therefore, as RTS1 is a polar RFB, it only blocks forks at this site in one orientation, which we refer to as the active orientation (AO) (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a property of the experimental system.

claim: The Ade+ recombinant frequencies at the 35 kb, 75 kb and 140 kb sites are essentially the same with and without RTS1-IO (p > 0.4).
source: Indeed, the Ade+ recombinant frequencies, measured at the 35 kb, 75 kb and 140 kb sites are essentially the same with and without RTS1-IO (p > 0.4)
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the 0 kb, 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb sites RTS1-IO causes only a modest ~1.4–1.9-fold increase in deletions (p ≤ 0.001) compared to the spontaneous frequencies obtained from equivalent strains with no RTS1.
source: and at the 0 kb, 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb sites RTS1-IO causes only a modest ~1.4–1.9-fold increase in deletions (p ≤ 0.001) compared to the spontaneous frequencies obtained from equivalent strains with no RTS1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Strains with RTS1-AO exhibited increases of between 32-fold to 133-fold in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at sites up to 35 kb downstream of the RFB.
source: Compared to strains with RTS1-IO, those with RTS1-AO exhibited increases of between 32-fold to 133-fold in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at sites up to 35 kb downstream of the RFB, but no increase was observed at the 75 kb and 140 kb sites (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No increase in Ade+ recombinants was observed at the 75 kb and 140 kb sites with RTS1-AO compared to RTS1-IO.
source: Compared to strains with RTS1-IO, those with RTS1-AO exhibited increases of between 32-fold to 133-fold in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at sites up to 35 kb downstream of the RFB, but no increase was observed at the 75 kb and 140 kb sites (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Convergence with a canonical replication fork limits the distance travelled by restarted replication and determines the chromosomal region in which TS can occur.
source: In our previous study, we showed that convergence with a canonical replication fork limits the distance travelled by restarted replication and, therefore, determines the chromosomal region in which TS can occur (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Deletion of ori-1253 had no effect on the frequency of spontaneous recombination at the 75 kb reporter (p = 0.58 and 0.34 for gene conversions and deletions, respectively).
source: This deletion had no effect on the frequency of spontaneous recombination at the 75 kb reporter (p = 0.58 and 0.34 for gene conversions and deletions, respectively)
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of ori-1253 caused an approximately 5-fold increase in deletions when RTS1-AO was present (p < 0.0001).
source: whereas it caused an approximately 5-fold increase in deletions when RTS1-AO was present (p < 0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Restarted replication can cause increased levels of TS at least as far as 75 kb downstream of a collapsed replication fork in S. pombe.
source: These data show that restarted replication can cause increased levels of TS at least as far as 75 kb downstream of a collapsed replication fork in S. pombe.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the 0 kb site, the fold increase in gene conversions is higher than that of deletions (by ~3:1).
source: However, at the 0 kb site, the fold increase in gene conversions is higher than that of deletions (by ~3:1)
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the 0.2 kb downstream site, the fold increases in gene conversions and deletions are comparable (126-fold and 135-fold, respectively).
source: whereas, at the 0.2 kb downstream site, the fold increases in gene conversions and deletions are comparable (126-fold and 135-fold, respectively)
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the 12.4 kb, 35 kb and 75 kb sites, the fold increase in deletions (42-fold, 58-fold and 4-fold, respectively) is much higher than for gene conversions (6-fold, 16-fold and 2-fold, respectively).
source: and, at the 12.4 kb, 35 kb and 75 kb sites, the fold increase in deletions (42-fold, 58-fold and 4-fold, respectively) is much higher than for gene conversions (6-fold, 16-fold and 2-fold, respectively).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During the initial phases of restarting DNA replication there is a greater likelihood of generating a gene conversion.
source: These data suggest that during the initial phases of restarting DNA replication there is a greater likelihood of generating a gene conversion, whereas the TS associated with restarted replication is more likely to give rise to a deletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of recombination events at different distances from RTS1.

claim: The TS associated with restarted replication is more likely to give rise to a deletion.
source: These data suggest that during the initial phases of restarting DNA replication there is a greater likelihood of generating a gene conversion, whereas the TS associated with restarted replication is more likely to give rise to a deletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of recombination events at different distances from RTS1.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, efficient BIR depends on the Pif1 DNA helicase, which aids D-loop migration.
source: In S. cerevisiae, efficient BIR depends on the Pif1 DNA helicase, which aids D-loop migration (Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: Pfh1 has an essential mitochondrial function in S. pombe.
source: This was important because Pfh1 has an essential mitochondrial function in S. pombe (Pinter et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pinter et al., 2008.

claim: In the case of pfh1-m21, there was little or no effect on the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at the three sites (0 kb, 0.2 kb, and 12.4 kb with RTS1-IO).
source: In the case of pfh1-m21, there was little or no effect on the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at the three sites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: pfh1-mt* has little effect on Ade+ recombinants at the 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb reporter sites with RTS1-IO.
source: The same is true for pfh1-mt* at the 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb reporter sites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When the repeats flank RTS1-IO, the pfh1-mt* mutant exhibits an approximately 3-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants, which are mostly (87%) deletions.
source: However, when the repeats flank RTS1-IO, the pfh1-mt* mutant exhibits an approximately 3-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants, which are mostly (87%) deletions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pfh1 might be needed for aiding non-recombinogenic DNA replication past RTS1-IO.
source: This increase is more than the 2-fold increase observed in the equivalent strain with no RTS1 (Steinacher et al., 2012), which suggests that Pfh1 might be needed for aiding non-recombinogenic DNA replication past RTS1-IO.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of recombination frequencies with and without RTS1-IO in pfh1-mt* mutants.

claim: A greater than 7-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants was observed in a pfh1-mt* mutant, compared to wild-type, when RTS1-AO is flanked by the repeats at the 0 kb site.
source: Consistent with previous data (Steinacher et al., 2012), we observed a greater than 7-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants in a pfh1-mt* mutant, compared to wild-type, when RTS1-AO is flanked by the repeats at the 0 kb site (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar increase in Ade+ recombinants was seen in a pfh1-m21 mutant at the 0 kb site with RTS1-AO.
source: A similar increase was seen in a pfh1-m21 mutant and, in both cases, essentially all of the additional recombinants were deletions (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants at the 0 kb site with RTS1-AO, essentially all of the additional recombinants were deletions.
source: A similar increase was seen in a pfh1-m21 mutant and, in both cases, essentially all of the additional recombinants were deletions (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequency of recombinants formed at the 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb reporter sites (by TS associated with replication restart) was reduced in both pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants.
source: In contrast, the frequency of recombinants formed at the 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb reporter sites (by TS associated with replication restart) was reduced in both mutants (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were bigger fold reductions in TS at the 12.4 kb reporter than at the 0.2 kb reporter in pfh1 mutants.
source: Importantly, there were bigger fold reductions at the 12.4 kb reporter than at the 0.2 kb reporter, and with the pfh1-mt* mutant compared to the pfh1-m21 mutant (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were bigger fold reductions in TS with the pfh1-mt* mutant compared to the pfh1-m21 mutant.
source: Importantly, there were bigger fold reductions at the 12.4 kb reporter than at the 0.2 kb reporter, and with the pfh1-mt* mutant compared to the pfh1-m21 mutant (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a dosage-sensitive requirement for Pfh1 in promoting TS recombination downstream of RTS1-AO.
source: These data show that there is a doseage-sensitive requirement for Pfh1 in promoting TS recombination downstream of RTS1-AO.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing differential effects of pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants.

claim: Replication forks accumulated at RTS1-AO in both wild-type and pfh1-mt* mutant.
source: As seen previously, replication forks accumulated at RTS1-AO in both wild-type and pfh1-mt* mutant (Figure 3B) (Steinacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to previous work.

claim: In wild-type, blocked forks at RTS1-AO were resolved through a mixture of restart (indicated by the presence of large Y-shaped molecules) and fork convergence at the RFB (indicated by the presence of double Y-shaped molecules).
source: However, whilst in the wild-type blocked forks were resolved through a mixture of restart (indicated by the presence of large Y-shaped molecules) and fork convergence at the RFB (indicated by the presence of double Y-shaped molecules)
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the pfh1-mt* mutant, blocked forks at RTS1-AO were resolved mainly by fork convergence (indicated by a reduction in large Y-shaped molecules and increase in double Y-shaped molecules).
source: in the pfh1-mt* mutant they were resolved mainly by fork convergence (indicated by a reduction in large Y-shaped molecules and increase in double Y-shaped molecules) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3C.

claim: Pfh1 promotes efficient replication restart following fork collapse at RTS1.
source: These data indicate that Pfh1 promotes efficient replication restart following fork collapse at RTS1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 2DGE data showing reduced restart in pfh1-mt* mutant.

claim: A novel DNA signal running approximately parallel to the ascending arc of small Y-shaped molecules accumulated in the pfh1-mt* mutant.
source: Intriguingly, we also observed the accumulation of a novel DNA signal running approximately parallel to the ascending arc of small Y-shaped molecules in the pfh1-mt* mutant (Figure 3B, labelled 'e' in the left hand panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A similar signal to that observed in pfh1-mt* was recently reported to accumulate in samples from rad51∆ and rad52∆ mutants, and was shown to depend on the 5' to 3' exonuclease Exo1.
source: A similar signal was recently reported to accumulate in samples from rad51∆ and rad52∆ mutants, and was shown to depend on the 5' to 3' exonuclease Exo1 (Ait Saada et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ait Saada et al., 2017.

claim: Rad51 and Rad52 protect the collapsed replication fork from excessive Exo1 activity, which could generate extensively resected regressed replication forks.
source: Based on these findings, it was proposed that Rad51 and Rad52 protect the collapsed replication fork from excessive Exo1 activity, which could generate extensively resected regressed replication forks (Ait Saada et al., 2017; Teixeira-Silva et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ait Saada et al., 2017 and Teixeira-Silva et al., 2017.

claim: The novel DNA signal from pfh1-mt* depended on Exo1.
source: To see if the novel DNA signal from pfh1-mt* depended on Exo1, we analysed replication intermediates from a pfh1-mt* exo1∆ double mutant (Figure 3B). This analysis showed that the novel signal was indeed Exo1 dependent.
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 3B comparing pfh1-mt* single and pfh1-mt* exo1∆ double mutants.

claim: The similarly low levels of large Y-shaped DNA molecules from both the pfh1-mt* single mutant and pfh1-mt* exo1∆ double mutant indicate that Pfh1 does not simply counter Exo1 activity to promote efficient RDR.
source: Regardless of the mechanism, the similarly low levels of large Y-shaped DNA molecules, from both the pfh1-mt* single mutant and pfh1-mt* exo1∆ double mutant, indicate that Pfh1 does not simply counter Exo1 activity to promote efficient RDR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 2DGE data comparing pfh1-mt* and pfh1-mt* exo1∆ mutants.

claim: In the control strains with RTS1-IO, a modest increase in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants was observed at the 0.2 kb reporter (but not 12.4 kb reporter) in both pfh1 mutants when ori-1253 was deleted.
source: In the control strains, with RTS1-IO, a modest increase in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants was observed at the 0.2 kb reporter (but not 12.4 kb reporter) in both pfh1 mutants, which might stem from fork collapse at RTS1-IO due to loss of Pfh1 'sweepase' activity (see Discussion) (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the strains with RTS1-AO and ori-1253 deleted, the frequency of Ade+ recombinants increased at both 0.2 kb and 12.4 kb reporter sites.
source: In the strains with RTS1-AO, the frequency of Ade+ recombinants increased at both reporter sites when ori-1253 was deleted
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In strains with RTS1-AO and ori-1253 deleted, whilst the frequency of gene conversions remained less in the pfh1 mutants than in wild-type, the overall number of recombinants in the pfh1-m21 mutant was more than 2-fold higher than wild-type at the 0.2 kb reporter due to a greater increase in deletions.
source: and, whilst the frequency of gene conversions remained less in the pfh1 mutants than in wild-type, the overall number of recombinants in the pfh1-m21 mutant was more than 2-fold higher than wild-type at the 0.2 kb reporter due to a greater increase in deletions (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pfh1, in addition to promoting RDR, also limits TS recombination.
source: These data indicate that Pfh1, in addition to promoting RDR, also limits TS recombination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased deletions in pfh1-m21 mutant when ori-1253 is deleted.

claim: Collisions between replication forks and RNA Polymerase III (Pol III) transcription complexes at tRNA genes are known to stall fork progression.
source: Collisions between replication forks and RNA Polymerase III (Pol III) transcription complexes at tRNA genes are known to stall fork progression (Deshpande and Newlon, 1996; Pryce et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Fork stalling at tRNA genes generally only elicits detectable changes in recombination when in conjunction with other genetic elements that perturb DNA replication, or when there are defects in the replication machinery.
source: However, unlike at RTS1, fork stalling at tRNA genes generally only elicits detectable changes in recombination when in conjunction with other genetic elements that perturb DNA replication, or when there are defects in the replication machinery (reviewed in McFarlane and Whitehall, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review and represents established knowledge.

claim: Loss of Pfh1 causes a ~ 27-fold increase in direct repeat recombination when DNA replication is stalled through head-on collision with transcription at a tRNA gene inserted between the DNA repeats.
source: For example, work from our lab previously showed that loss of Pfh1 causes a ~ 27-fold increase in direct repeat recombination when DNA replication is stalled through head-on collision with transcription at a tRNA gene inserted between the DNA repeats (Steinacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: In the absence of RTS1-AO, there was little difference in the recombination frequency between strains with and without tRNAGLU08CD.
source: In the absence of RTS1-AO, there was little difference in the recombination frequency between strains with and without tRNAGLU08CD, whereas with tRNAGLU08HO there was a modest 1.5-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the absence of RTS1-AO, with tRNAGLU08HO there was a modest 1.5-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants.
source: In the absence of RTS1-AO, there was little difference in the recombination frequency between strains with and without tRNAGLU08CD, whereas with tRNAGLU08HO there was a modest 1.5-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In strains with RTS1-AO, the fold increase in Ade+ recombinants with tRNAGLU08HO was 2.3-fold.
source: A similar pattern was seen in the strains with RTS1-AO, although in this case the fold increase in Ade+ recombinants with tRNAGLU08HO was higher (2.3-fold) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Head-on collision between a restarted replication complex and a Pol III complex can trigger TS.
source: These data indicate that head-on collision between a restarted replication complex and a Pol III complex can trigger TS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased recombination with tRNAGLU08HO.

claim: In the absence of RTS1, both pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants caused a marked increase in Ade+ recombinants (17.3-fold and 31.6-fold, respectively) with tRNAGLU08HO.
source: In the absence of RTS1, both pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants caused a marked increase in Ade+ recombinants (17.3-fold and 31.6-fold, respectively) consistent with previous findings (Steinacher et al., 2012) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and a citation to previous work.

claim: In the presence of RTS1-AO, the fold change in TS in pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants compared to wild-type was essentially the same with and without tRNAGLU08HO.
source: However, in the presence of RTS1-AO, the fold change in TS in pfh1-m21 and pfh1-mt* mutants compared to wild-type was essentially the same with and without tRNAGLU08HO (compare data in Figure 2B and Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 5D.

claim: Pfh1 is not needed to suppress TS induced by head-on collision between a restarted replication complex and a Pol III complex.
source: These data suggest that Pfh1 is not needed to suppress TS induced by head-on collision between a restarted replication complex and a Pol III complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing TS with and without tRNAGLU08HO in pfh1 mutants.

claim: The RecQ family DNA helicase Rqh1 has been shown to limit ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB.
source: The RecQ family DNA helicase Rqh1 has been shown to limit ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB (Ahn et al., 2005; Lambert et al., 2010; Lorenz et al., 2009; Pietrobon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Analysis of rqh1∆ mutant revealed a 2.9-fold increase in recombinants at the 12.4 kb reporter site, indicating that Rqh1 plays a role in limiting TS.
source: To investigate whether it also affects TS associated with restarted DNA replication, we compared the frequency of Ade+ recombinants in a wild-type and rqh1∆ mutant at the 12.4 kb reporter site (Figure 6C). This analysis revealed a 2.9-fold increase in recombinants in the mutant, indicating that Rqh1 plays a role in limiting TS.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The fold increase in recombinants at 12.4 kb in rqh1∆ is similar to that for spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter site.
source: However, whereas the fold increase in recombinants at 12.4 kb is similar to that for spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter site (Figure 6A,C)
evidence: This statement is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: The fold increase in recombinants at 12.4 kb in rqh1∆ is significantly less than the 10-fold increase seen at the 0 kb site when RTS1-AO is flanked by the ade6- repeats.
source: it is significantly less than the 10-fold increase seen at the 0 kb site when RTS1-AO is flanked by the ade6- repeats (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rqh1 is not required for replication restart at RTS1.
source: Rqh1 is not required for replication restart at RTS1 (Lambert et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lambert et al., 2010.

claim: Rqh1 plays a more important role in limiting ectopic recombination during replication restart than in controlling TS associated with restarted replication.
source: and, therefore, the lower fold increase in recombinants at the 12.4 kb reporter site, compared to the 0 kb site, suggests that Rqh1 plays a more important role in limiting ectopic recombination during replication restart than in controlling TS associated with restarted replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of rqh1∆ at different reporter positions.

claim: It has been proposed that Rqh1 limits ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB by unwinding D-loops formed by Rad51, and that this activity is counteracted by chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1).
source: It has been proposed that Rqh1 limits ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB by unwinding D-loops formed by Rad51, and that this activity is counteracted by chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF1) (Pietrobon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pietrobon et al., 2014.

claim: Analysis of null mutants of two of the three CAF1 subunits (Pcf2 and Pcf3) reveals little or no change in spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter.
source: Our analysis of null mutants of two of the three CAF1 subunits (Pcf2 and Pcf3) reveals little or no change in spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: pcf2∆ and pcf3∆ mutants show an approximately 3-fold reduction in gene conversions and ~30% reduction in deletions when RTS1-AO is present at the 0 kb site.
source: but an approximately 3-fold reduction in gene conversions and ~30% reduction in deletions when RTS1-AO is present (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 2-fold reduction in gene conversions and a 4-fold reduction in deletions was observed in both pcf2∆ and pcf3∆ mutants downstream of RTS1-AO at the 12.4 kb reporter.
source: We also observed a 2-fold reduction in gene conversions and a 4-fold reduction in deletions in both pcf2∆ and pcf3∆ mutants downstream of RTS1-AO at the 12.4 kb reporter (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CAF1 promotes ectopic recombination associated with restarting replication at the RTS1 RFB.
source: These data confirm that CAF1 promotes ectopic recombination associated with restarting replication at the RTS1 RFB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced recombination in CAF1 mutants.

claim: CAF1 is not required for replication restart.
source: Moreover, considering that CAF1 is not required for replication restart (Pietrobon et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pietrobon et al., 2014.

claim: CAF1 promotes TS associated with restarted replication.
source: our data show that it also promotes TS associated with restarted replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced TS in CAF1 mutants at the 12.4 kb reporter.

claim: The DNA helicases Srs2 and Fbh1 are known regulators of Rad51-mediated recombination, especially at sites of replication fork stalling and collapse.
source: The DNA helicases Srs2 and Fbh1, which are members of the UvrD family of proteins, are known regulators of Rad51-mediated recombination, especially at sites of replication fork stalling and collapse (Chiolo et al., 2007; Fugger et al., 2009; Lorenz et al., 2009; Marini and Krejci, 2010; Morishita et al., 2005; Osman et al., 2005; Simandlova et al., 2013; Tsutsui et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: A previous study showed that both Srs2 and Fbh1 limit ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB.
source: Although a previous study showed that both proteins limit ectopic recombination at the RTS1 RFB (Lorenz et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lorenz et al., 2009.

claim: In the case of srs2∆, there was a similar 6-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants at both 0 kb and 12.4 kb reporters.
source: In the case of srs2∆, there was a similar 6-fold increase in Ade+ recombinants at both 0 kb and 12.4 kb reporters, which was also similar to the fold increase in spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter containing RTS1-IO (Figure 6A,B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and 6C.

claim: fbh1∆ does not exhibit an increase in spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter.
source: Unlike a srs2∆ mutant, fbh1∆ does not exhibit an increase in spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter (Figure 6A) (Lorenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Lorenz et al., 2009.

claim: When RTS1-AO is present, fbh1∆ causes an even greater increase in Ade+ recombinants at both 0 kb and 12.4 kb reporters than srs2∆.
source: However, when RTS1-AO is present, fbh1∆ causes an even greater increase in Ade+ recombinants at both 0 kb and 12.4 kb reporters than srs2∆ (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Both Srs2 and Fbh1 strongly inhibit TS recombination associated with restarted replication.
source: Altogether these data show that both Srs2 and Fbh1 strongly inhibit TS recombination associated with restarted replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased TS in srs2∆ and fbh1∆ mutants.

claim: It has been reported that Srs2 is needed to promote efficient replication restart at RTS1.
source: It has been reported that Srs2 is needed to promote efficient replication restart at RTS1 (Inagawa et al., 2009; Lambert et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Inagawa et al., 2009 and Lambert et al., 2010.

claim: The increase in TS observed at the 12.4 kb reporter in a srs2∆ mutant may be an underestimate of Srs2's importance in suppressing TS.
source: and, therefore, the increase in TS we observe at the 12.4 kb reporter in a srs2∆ mutant may be an underestimate of Srs2's importance in suppressing TS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of Srs2 in promoting restart.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the FANCM-related DNA helicase Mph1 and structure-specific nuclease Mus81 have both been shown to affect levels of TS associated with BIR, with the former promoting TS and the latter limiting it.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the FANCM-related DNA helicase Mph1 and structure-specific nuclease Mus81 have both been shown to affect levels of TS associated with BIR, with the former promoting TS and the latter limiting it (Mayle et al., 2015; Stafa et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mayle et al., 2015 and Stafa et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of fml1 results in an almost 10-fold reduction in gene conversions at the 0 kb reporter whilst the frequency of deletions remains unchanged.
source: As reported previously, loss of fml1 results in an almost 10-fold reduction in gene conversions at the 0 kb reporter whilst the frequency of deletions remains unchanged (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and a citation to Sun et al., 2008.

claim: Spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter is similarly affected by fml1∆, albeit the fold reduction in gene conversions (~2.6-fold) is not as great.
source: Spontaneous recombination at the 0 kb reporter is similarly affected by fml1∆, albeit the fold reduction in gene conversions (~2.6-fold) is not as great (Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is little change in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at the 12.4 kb reporter downstream of RTS1-AO in fml1∆.
source: In contrast, there is little change in the frequency of Ade+ recombinants at the 12.4 kb reporter downstream of RTS1-AO (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of mus81 has no effect on the frequency of gene conversions at either 0 or 12.4 kb reporters.
source: Deletion of mus81 has no effect on the frequency of gene conversions at either 0 or 12.4 kb reporters
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Deletion of mus81 causes a slight increase in deletions (~1.4-fold) at the 0 kb reporter.
source: but does cause a slight increase in deletions (~1.4-fold) at the 0 kb reporter
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletion of mus81 causes a decrease in deletions (~1.5-fold) at the 12.4 kb reporter.
source: and a decrease in deletions (~1.5-fold) at the 12.4 kb reporter (Figure 6BC, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 2DGE of replication intermediates at and around RTS1-AO reveals wild-type levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules in fml1∆ and mus81∆ mutants, suggesting that restart is unaffected by loss of either Fml1 or Mus81.
source: However, 2DGE of replication intermediates at and around RTS1-AO reveals wild-type levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules, suggesting that restart is unaffected by loss of either Fml1 or Mus81 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by 2DGE data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The collapsed replication fork regresses to form a classic 'chicken foot' structure with an exposed ssDNA tail formed by the nucleolytic activity of the Mre11-Rad50-Nbs1-Ctp1 complex and Exo1.
source: We envisage that the collapsed replication fork regresses to form a classic 'chicken foot' structure with an exposed ssDNA tail formed by the nucleolytic activity of the Mre11-Rad50-Nbs1-Ctp1 complex and Exo1 (Figure 7, step 1) (Teixeira-Silva et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Rad51 loads onto the ssDNA tail to form a nucleoprotein filament that first locates a homologous duplex and then invades it to form a D-loop.
source: Rad51 loads onto the ssDNA tail to form a nucleoprotein filament that first locates a homologous duplex and then invades it to form a D-loop (Figure 7, step 2).
evidence: This is part of the model proposed by the authors based on established knowledge.

claim: Pol∂ extends the 3' end of the invading strand.
source: Pol∂ extends the 3' end of the invading strand (Miyabe et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miyabe et al., 2015 and is part of the model.

claim: As Pol∂ extends the 3' end of the invading strand, the D-loop moves in tandem.
source: and, as it does, the D-loop moves in tandem (Figure 7, step 3) (Saini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saini et al., 2013 and is part of the model.

claim: RDR, triggered by fork collapse at RTS1, is semi-conservative.
source: Such a model would be compatible with the finding that RDR, triggered by fork collapse at RTS1, is semi-conservative (Miyabe et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miyabe et al., 2015.

claim: BIR is conservative.
source: and contrasts with BIR, which is conservative (Donnianni and Symington, 2013; Saini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Donnianni and Symington, 2013 and Saini et al., 2013.

claim: As DNA replication progresses, the associated migrating D-loop is likely to be susceptible to dissociation, either through the action of DNA helicases and/or by branch migration of the regressed replication fork 'catching up' with it.
source: As DNA replication progresses, the associated migrating D-loop is likely to be susceptible to dissociation, either through the action of DNA helicases and/or by branch migration of the regressed replication fork 'catching up' with it (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: Dissociation of the D-loop in a region of repetitive DNA would lead to TS if the ejected DNA strand re-invades the 'wrong' repeat.
source: Dissociation of the D-loop in a region of repetitive DNA would lead to TS if the ejected DNA strand re-invades the 'wrong' repeat (Figure 7, steps 4 and 5; note that the DNA repeats, in yellow, are directly orientated as they are in our genetic assay).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors to explain TS.

claim: TS associated with BIR in S. cerevisiae is thought to reflect an inherent instability of the migrating D-loop, which has evolved to encourage DSB repair by synthesis-dependent strand annealing.
source: TS associated with BIR in S. cerevisiae is thought to reflect an inherent instability of the migrating D-loop, which has evolved to encourage DSB repair by synthesis-dependent strand annealing (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2007.

claim: The observation that TS in S. cerevisae is constrained to the first 10 kb of template DNA that is copied, suggests that the D-loop eventually matures into a more stable structure.
source: The observation that TS in S. cerevisae is constrained to the first 10 kb of template DNA that is copied, suggests that the D-loop eventually matures into a more stable structure (Mayle et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations from cited studies.

claim: D-loop maturation may involve cleavage of the D-loop by structure-specific nucleases such as Mus81.
source: This maturation process may involve cleavage of the D-loop by structure-specific nucleases such as Mus81 (Mayle et al., 2015; Osman and Whitby, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The finding that TS downstream of RTS1-AO is generally biased in favour of deletions, whereas at the RFB gene conversions predominate, suggests that the frequency of double TS events declines soon after replication has restarted.
source: Our finding that TS downstream of RTS1-AO is generally biased in favour of deletions, whereas at the RFB gene conversions predominate, suggests that the frequency of double TS events declines soon after replication has restarted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing different patterns of recombination at different positions.

claim: Carr and colleagues reported that the propensity for restarted replication to perform a U-turn at small inverted repeats positioned downstream of RTS1 declined 4-fold when the distance between RFB and repeats was increased from 0 to 2 kb, and then appeared to plateau.
source: Interestingly, Carr and colleagues reported that the propensity for restarted replication to perform a U-turn at small inverted repeats positioned downstream of RTS1 declined 4-fold when the distance between RFB and repeats was increased from 0 to 2 kb, and then appeared to plateu (Mizuno et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mizuno et al., 2013.

claim: The putative migrating D-loop, which is formed following replication fork collapse at RTS1-AO, undergoes partial stabilization shortly after it is formed.
source: These observations suggest that the putative migrating D-loop, which is formed following replication fork collapse at RTS1-AO, undergoes partial stabilization shortly after it is formed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations about TS patterns and U-turn frequencies.

claim: A degree of D-loop instability must be retained because TS can be detected over distances of at least 75 kb downstream of the site of fork collapse.
source: However, unlike with BIR in S. cerevisiae, a degree of D-loop instability must be retained because we can detect TS over distances of at least 75 kb downstream of the site of fork collapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing TS at 75 kb.

claim: Head-on collisions with transcription complexes might exacerbate D-loop instability and be a key trigger in promoting TS.
source: Our finding, that tRNAGLU08HO increases TS downstream of RTS1-AO, suggests that head-on collisions with transcription complexes might exacerbate D-loop instability and be a key trigger in promoting TS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased TS with tRNAGLU08HO.

claim: The apparent disparity in D-loop maturation, between BIR in S. cerevisiae and RDR in S. pombe, may reflect differences in D-loop processing.
source: The apparent disparity in D-loop maturation, between BIR in S. cerevisiae and RDR in S. pombe, may reflect differences in D-loop processing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanistic differences.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Mus81 constrains TS during BIR presumably by resolving the D-loop into a more stable fork structure.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Mus81 constrains TS during BIR presumably by resolving the D-loop into a more stable fork structure (Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: In S. pombe, there is no evidence that Mus81 is required to constrain TS during RDR.
source: However, in S. pombe, we found no evidence that Mus81 is required to constrain TS during RDR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no major effect of mus81∆ on TS.

claim: The only constraint over the region in which TS can occur in S. pombe seems to be the point at which the restarted replication converges with the oncoming replication fork.
source: In fact the only constraint, over the region in which TS can occur in S. pombe, seems to be the point at which the restarted replication converges with the oncoming replication fork - a property which is shared with BIR in S. cerevisiae (Mayle et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: TS associated with restarted replication is thought to be responsible for generating many of the genome rearrangements that are associated with cancer and other disease states.
source: TS associated with restarted replication is thought to be responsible for generating many of the genome rearrangements that are associated with cancer and other disease states (Carvalho and Lupski, 2016; Hastings et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Some complex genome rearrangements can span distances of hundreds of kilobases and could not be formed from a single restarted replication event if TS was limited to a 10 kb region downstream of the site of fork collapse.
source: However, some complex genome rearrangements can span distances of hundreds of kilobases and, therefore, could not be formed from a single restarted replication event if TS was limited to a 10 kb region downstream of the site of fork collapse (Hastings et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of complex genome rearrangements and supported by a citation.

claim: TS, associated with the repair of a single collapsed replication fork, may be capable of generating some of the long-range and complex genome rearrangements seen in humans.
source: Our finding, that TS events occur over a much greater distance in S. pombe than they do for BIR in S. cerevisiae, shows that TS, associated with the repair of a single collapsed replication fork, may be capable of generating some of the long-range and complex genome rearrangements seen in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing TS over long distances in S. pombe.

claim: Similar to BIR in S. cerevisiae, the Pif1 family DNA helicase Pfh1 promotes RDR.
source: Similar to BIR in S. cerevisiae, the Pif1 family DNA helicase Pfh1 promotes RDR, which explains why there is a general reduction in the levels of TS downstream of RTS1-AO in pfh1-m21 and -mt* mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced TS in pfh1 mutants.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Pif1 aids DNA synthesis during BIR by driving D-loop migration.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Pif1 aids DNA synthesis during BIR by driving D-loop migration (Wilson et al., 2013), and Pfh1 might do likewise during RDR in S. pombe.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: Pfh1 might aid DNA synthesis during RDR in S. pombe by driving D-loop migration.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Pif1 aids DNA synthesis during BIR by driving D-loop migration (Wilson et al., 2013), and Pfh1 might do likewise during RDR in S. pombe.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy with Pif1 in S. cerevisiae.

claim: Pfh1 is a candidate for promoting the putative branch migration and/or re-setting of the regressed replication fork behind the migrating D-loop.
source: Moreover, our observation, that resected regressed replication forks accumulate at RTS1-AO in a pfh1-mt* mutant, suggests that Pfh1 is a candidate for promoting the putative branch migration and/or re-setting of the regressed replication fork behind the migrating D-loop (see Discussion above).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of resected forks in pfh1-mt* mutant.

claim: Pfh1 has the ability to drive DNA replication by dislodging protein-DNA barriers via its so-called sweepase activity.
source: Pfh1 also has the ability to drive DNA replication by dislodging protein-DNA barriers via its so-called sweepase activity (Sabouri et al., 2012; Steinacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sabouri et al., 2012 and Steinacher et al., 2012.

claim: Efficient RDR past RTS1 presumably requires removal of the barrier protein Rtf1, which may depend on Pfh1's sweepase activity.
source: Efficient RDR past RTS1 presumably requires removal of the barrier protein Rtf1, which may depend on Pfh1's sweepase activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which Pfh1 promotes RDR.

claim: The finding that Pfh1 suppresses TS contrasts with BIR in S. cerevisisae where Pif1 has no affect on TS.
source: This finding contrasts with BIR in S. cerevisisae where Pif1 has no affect on TS (Stafa et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stafa et al., 2014.

claim: S. cerevisiae has a second Pif1 helicase called Rrm3, which, whilst seemingly not required for BIR, is important for the repair of replication-associated DSBs as well as replication past stable protein-DNA complexes.
source: Unlike S. pombe and humans, which have only one Pif1 family helicase, S. cerevisiae has a second Pif1 helicase called Rrm3, which, whilst seemingly not required for BIR, is important for the repair of replication-associated DSBs as well as replication past stable protein-DNA complexes (Ivessa et al., 2003; Muñoz-Galván et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: It is possible that Pif1 and Rrm3 act redundantly in the suppression of TS in S. cerevisiae.
source: It is possible that Pif1 and Rrm3 act redundantly in the suppression of TS in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible explanation for the difference between S. pombe and S. cerevisiae.

claim: The role of Pif1 helicases in suppressing TS may only be evident when RDR acts during S-phase alongside ongoing canonical DNA replication.
source: Alternatively, the role of Pif1 helicases in suppressing TS may only be evident when RDR acts during S-phase alongside ongoing canonical DNA replication.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about when the role of Pif1 helicases in suppressing TS might be observed.

claim: Pfh1 may play an important role in directing the termination of DNA replication where a canonical fork encounters a D-loop.
source: Specifically, they may play an important role in directing the termination of DNA replication where a canonical fork encounters a D-loop.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the role of Pfh1.

claim: Pfh1 drives D-loop dissociation during termination through its action as an accessory helicase at the oncoming DNA replication fork, where it likely translocates on the lagging template strand in a 5' – 3' direction.
source: We speculate that Pfh1 drives D-loop dissociation during termination through its action as an accessory helicase at the oncoming DNA replication fork, where it likely translocates on the lagging template strand in a 5' – 3' direction (i.e. towards the D-loop and on the same DNA strand that the invading strand is annealed to) (Sabouri, 2017) (Figure 7, step 7b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which Pfh1 suppresses TS, supported by a citation.

claim: Without Pfh1 activity, there would be a greater tendency for the 3' end of the invading strand at the D-loop to ligate to the lagging strand of the oncoming fork, which would specifically favour deletion formation.
source: Without this activity there would be a greater tendancy for the 3' end of the invading strand at the D-loop to ligate to the lagging strand of the oncoming fork, which would specifically favour deletion formation in our genetic assay (Figure 7, steps 7a – 9a).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequence of losing Pfh1 activity.

claim: In the instances where an increase in Ade+ recombinants is detected when pfh1 is mutated, it is specifically deletions that increase, with the frequency of gene conversions either decreasing or remaining unchanged.
source: Indeed, in the instances where we can detect an increase in Ade+ recombinants when pfh1 is mutated, it is specifically deletions that increase, with the frequency of gene conversions either decreasing or remaining unchanged (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Rqh1, Srs2 and Fbh1, and their homologues in other organisms, are well known as major players in directing the outcome of homologous recombination reactions.
source: These helicases, and their homologues in other organisms, are well known as major players in directing the outcome of homologous recombination reactions (Doe and Whitby, 2004; Fugger et al., 2009; Kohzaki et al., 2007; Larsen and Hickson, 2013; Lorenz et al., 2009; Morishita et al., 2005; Niu and Klein, 2017; Osman et al., 2005; Simandlova et al., 2013; Tsutsui et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: The homologue of Rqh1 in S. cerevisiae (Sgs1) might limit translocations between highly diverged genes by suppressing TS during BIR.
source: However, their role in suppressing TS downstream of a collapsed replication fork has not previously been demonstrated, though it has been suggested that the homologue of Rqh1 in S. cerevisiae (Sgs1) might limit translocations between highly diverged genes by suppressing TS during BIR (Schmidt et al., 2006).

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: The dissociation of a nascent D-loop can abort a TS event before a genetic change is made.
source: The dissociation of a nascent D-loop can abort a TS event before a genetic change is made (e.g. a deletion or gene conversion in our genetic assay) and, therefore, the loss of this activity might account for the increase in TS we observe in both rqh1∆ and srs2∆ mutants (Figure 5).

claim: Lambert and colleagues showed that Rqh1 was responsible for the disappearance of recombination intermediates at RTS1 in cells lacking CAF1, and proposed that this was due to its ability to drive D-loop dissociation.

claim: Rqh1 may affect TS by catalyzing the branch migration of the regressed replication fork behind the migrating D-loop.

claim: Several RecQ–type helicases have been shown to unwind/branch migrate four-way/Holliday junctions in vitro.
source: The regressed fork forms a four-way/Holliday junction, which is a structure that several RecQ–type helicases have been shown to unwind/branch migrate in vitro (Cejka and Kowalczykowski, 2010; Karow et al., 2000; LeRoy et al., 2005; Machwe et al., 2011).

claim: Branch migration of the four-way junction into the 'back' of the D-loop would cause the D-loop to unwind.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequence of branch migration.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Anand et al., 2014.
